extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, law & economics researchers, USPTO policymakers, and empirical IP researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of how patent examiner characteristics (experience, prior-art search intensity, tenure, incentives) relate to the probability an application is granted and to prosecution rigor (rejections/amendments). Uses January 2001 U.S. utility application cohort and measures constructed from PAIR, patent front pages, employee directories, and EPO outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, industrial applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step/non--obviousness, and (3) be industrially applicable. Examiners are charged with serving as gatekeepers to ensure that only novel and non--obvious inventions are granted patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the substantive standard examiners apply when assessing applications; failing to meet these criteria should lead to rejections. (Background legal standard used throughout the analysis.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor / applicant disclosure of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, applicants have a duty of candor to disclose any previous patents and publications, or 'prior art,' that are material to patentability. Most (but not all) applicants disclose patent and non--patent prior art as part of their application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there is a duty to disclose, there is no affirmative requirement that applicants conduct prior-art searches; incentives for applicants to search vary across inventions and industries. Applicant disclosures are part of the set of references examiners consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner prior-art search intensity (US_SHARE)
rubrics_metrics.description: US_SHARE: the average share (over patents issued by an examiner during 2001--2006) of citations to prior U.S. patents that were provided by the examiner rather than the applicant — used as a proxy for how thoroughly an examiner searches patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed from citations in patents issued by the examiner; more precise for examiners who issued many patents. Models exclude applications where the examiner issued fewer than ten patents over 2001--2006 when using these measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner prior-art search intensity (NP_SHARE)
rubrics_metrics.description: NP_SHARE: analogous measure for non--patent prior art (share of citations to non--patent literature provided by the examiner rather than the applicant) — used as proxy for examiner searching of non--patent literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non--patent prior art is harder to find and examiners tend to contribute a much smaller share; NP_SHARE is heavily skewed toward applicant submission in many fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner experience (years in USPTO; cohort categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience measured as difference between the year examiner first appears in the Employee Directory and the year the application is docketed to the examiner; analyzed non-parametrically using cohorts: 0-1 years, 2-4 years, 5-7 years, and 8+ years (right-censored due to directories pre-1992).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience is a primary independent variable. Authors find more experienced examiners are more likely to grant patents (effect plateaus after 7 years). Experience is correlated with tenure/signatory authority and is right-censored; models include cohort dummies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant probability / patent grant rate (main dependent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an application filed in January 2001 was granted by June 2008 (used as the primary outcome variable relating to examiner characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated with linear probability models including over 300 art-unit fixed effects and robust standard errors clustered on examiners; used to assess the relationship between examiner characteristics and the key USPTO decision to grant or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-action allowance / issuance without any rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator for applications that were issued on the first office action (no non--final or final examiner rejections during prosecution) — used as a measure of prosecution rigor or lack thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as absence of narrowing negotiation; experienced examiners have higher probability of first-action allowances. Used as auxiliary dependent variable to probe mechanisms behind grant-rate differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether prosecution involved any examiner rejections (proxy for narrowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary indicator from PAIR data whether the prosecution ever included an examiner rejection (non--final or final). Authors use this as a measure of whether the prosecution process compelled narrowing/amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used instead of raw claim-count changes because number-of-claims is an imperfect proxy for scope; rejections are a more direct signal that examiner compelled amendment or negotiation occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in number of claims as a measure of scope (flagged as problematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change in number of claims between the application and the issued patent is a candidate measure of narrowing of scope, but it is problematic because number-of-claims can increase for tactical reasons and does not consistently indicate scope narrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors show many granted applications with rejections still exhibit no net decrease (and sometimes increases) in claim counts; therefore they caution against using claim-count change alone as evidence of narrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-level observable controls for selection tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable application characteristics used to test for selection/sorting include: number of pages in application, patent family size (number of countries in which filed), number of applicant-provided patent references, number of applicant-provided non--patent references, and applicant prior patent volume (patents issued in prior year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'time-zero' measures are used to test whether SPEs sort applications by patent-worthiness across examiners. Authors find little evidence of sorting on these observables (effects are small or insignificant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-unit assignment rules and potential sorting (MPEP sec.903.08(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are divided into technology classes (art units), and Supervisory Patent Examiners (SPEs) assign applications to examiners based on a loose set of rules (familiarity with technology, docket flow management), per MPEP guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews and data suggest assignment is driven more by familiarity and docket flow than by pre-assessing patent-worthiness. Sorting on quality would require SPEs to judge patent-worthiness at intake, which evidence does not support.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO grant/reject status as an external proxy for patent-worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same application (single-priority applications subset) was also filed at the European Patent Office and whether it was granted or rejected there — used as an external benchmark of patent-worthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model specifications control for EPO status; conditioning on EPO outcomes, the experience and search-intensity effects persist, arguing against simple assignment-selection bias. Authors caution EPO is not a gold standard but is informative for selection tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner incentives: counts/quotas, promotion and bonus structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners' promotions and bonuses are tied to 'counts' accumulated for first office actions and disposals (grants or abandonments); activities like searching, compelling amendments, or issuing final rejections are not rewarded by the count system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This incentive structure may bias examiners toward granting (or quick disposals) rather than exhaustive searching or rejecting; counts-per-hour expectations vary by art and grade and increase with pay grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure / signatory authority and its effect on scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: After promotion to GS-14 (generally 4–6 years) examiners receive signatory authority (right to sign off independently). Junior examiners are subject to more review by senior examiners. Tenure is strongly correlated with experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tenure may reduce scrutiny and contribute to higher grant rates among more experienced examiners; authors find tenure correlated with experience but cannot cleanly separate tenure effects from experience effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective retention / attrition as a potential confound
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis that more diligent/thorough examiners may leave the USPTO earlier (selective retention), which could make the remaining experienced cohort look less thorough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors test attrition using employee directories and measures of search intensity; results give little evidence that selective retention fully explains the experience effects on grant rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search difficulty for non--patent literature (NPL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non--patent literature is less accessible, less standardized, and often harder to identify and comprehend compared to patents; examiners generally contribute a much smaller share of NPL citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains low NP_SHARE averages and why searching NPL is costlier/time-consuming; supports interpreting NP_SHARE differences as meaningful for examination rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and workload constraints per application
rubrics_metrics.description: Although prosecution can take 3–4 years on average, examiners spend on average only about 18 hours over those years working on any given application; high workload and time pressure constrain thoroughness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps explain practical limits to exhaustive prior-art searching and why examiner behavior (search intensity, quicker allowances) may be driven by resource constraints and quotas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical model choices and controls (art-unit fixed effects, clustering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear probability models include fixed effects for each of over 300 art units, robust standard errors clustered on examiners, and exclusion rules when measuring search-intensity for low-volume examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modeling choices are the authors' approach to isolate examiner effects from art-unit heterogeneity and to account for within-examiner correlation in outcomes.
